title: I wanted a clock that never needed setting. Things escalated.
gist: Ars Technica's Senior Technology Editor builds a custom self-setting bedside clock (Raspberry Pi, Adafruit seven-segment LED display, HomeKit, systemd, Gitea CI/CD), leaning on Claude Code (Opus 4.8, then Anthropic's 'Fable' model) for nearly all the Python and CAD/Fusion work he couldn't do himself; he also tests a locally-hosted quantized Qwen 3.6-35B model on a GB10-powered Acer Veriton controlling Autodesk Fusion via its new MCP server, finding it 'almost' capable but ultimately falling back to Claude Code/Fable for the harder CAD edits.

themes.theme: LLM coding agents as project enablers

insights.claim: The author explicitly states he would not have finished the DIY clock project without an LLM's help, since his own Python skills and patience for troubleshooting via StackOverflow were insufficient for the I2C display-communication code required.
insights.speaker: Lee Hutchinson
insights.so_what: A concrete first-person account of an experienced enterprise IT professional (not a novice) being unable to complete a moderate coding task without an AI coding agent — evidence of LLM coding tools expanding the practical scope of hobbyist/engineer projects.
insights.quote: I know this admission may be anathema to many among the Ars commentariat, but it is what it is—without the LLM, I wouldn't have finished the project.

insights.claim: The author used Claude Code with Anthropic's Opus 4.8 model first, then switched to a newer model he calls 'Fable,' describing Fable's coding capability on this intern-level project as overkill, 'like unleashing the full power of the Death Star on a mosquito.'
insights.speaker: Lee Hutchinson
insights.so_what: A real-world, non-benchmark data point that Anthropic's newest 'Fable' model is perceived by an experienced user as substantially more capable than needed for routine coding tasks — relevant color for gauging frontier-model capability trajectory and cost-efficiency tradeoffs in coding use cases.
insights.quote: Claude Code proved more than capable enough to tackle this project—first with Opus 4.8 and then later with the new fancy Fable model, whose world-ending powers I harnessed and used on what is probably in truth an intern-level coding project.
insights.locator: section '"You taught me language; and my profit on't is, I know how to code"'

insights.claim: Beyond core application code, the author had the LLM handle the HomeKit integration, the install/deployment routine, specifics of the CI/CD pipeline, and most of the project's repo documentation.
insights.speaker: Lee Hutchinson
insights.so_what: Illustrates LLM coding agents now handling not just isolated functions but end-to-end auxiliary engineering work (docs, deployment, integrations) — a broadening of the tasks non-specialist users delegate to AI.
insights.quote: The LLM did such a good job that I also had it do the HomeKit integration, the install routine, some specifics around the deployment pipeline, and most of the repo documentation.

themes.theme: Local/edge model inference vs. frontier cloud models

insights.claim: The author tested a locally-hosted, quantized Qwen 3.6-35B-A3B-NVFP4 model running on a GB10-powered Acer Veriton GN100 (a device he is separately reviewing) to control Autodesk Fusion's CAD software via its new MCP server, using the OpenCode tool.
insights.speaker: Lee Hutchinson
insights.so_what: A concrete example of local, quantized open-weight models being tested as agentic controllers for professional design software via MCP — a real data point on the maturing local-inference-plus-MCP stack that could reduce reliance on cloud frontier models for narrow tasks.
insights.quote: But Fusion now ships with an MCP server, so I could potentially let an LLM remote control the application and make the modifications for me.

insights.claim: The locally-hosted Qwen 3.6 model was 'almost up to the task' of modifying the 3D-printed clock enclosure in Fusion, successfully making one requested change but failing another, forcing the author to fall back to Claude Code and Fable to complete the CAD modifications.
insights.speaker: Lee Hutchinson
insights.so_what: A direct head-to-head anecdote where a frontier cloud model (Fable) succeeded where a local open-weight model partially failed on an agentic CAD-editing task — useful signal on the current capability gap between local and frontier models for tool-use/agentic work.
insights.quote: Qwen 3.6 was almost up to the task, making one of my changes but flubbing the other; I fell back on Claude Code and Fable to handle most of the model adjustments.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'The answer turned out to be'

insights.claim: The author found the local Qwen model experiment intriguing enough to say he will return to it in a future dedicated piece, suggesting ongoing interest in evaluating local model capability for design/engineering tasks.
insights.speaker: Lee Hutchinson
insights.so_what: Signals continued editorial coverage of local-model viability for agentic tool-use is likely from this author/outlet, worth tracking as a recurring data point on local-vs-cloud model competitiveness.
insights.quote: Still, the local model was intriguing, and I'll be returning to it in a future piece.
insights.locator: end of section 'Full fathom five Autodesk lies'

themes.theme: DIY hardware and self-hosted infrastructure choices

insights.claim: The author chose a Raspberry Pi over an Arduino-class microcontroller specifically for the Debian-based OS, built-in Wi-Fi/NTP support, and familiar Linux remote-management tooling, but notes Raspberry Pi units of any flavor are 'extremely scarce right now.'
insights.speaker: Lee Hutchinson
insights.so_what: A firsthand supply-constraint data point on Raspberry Pi availability, relevant to anyone tracking single-board-computer/maker-hardware supply chains.
insights.quote: Raspberry Pi units of any flavor are extremely scarce right now, so someone with better coding chops or with a more outsized sense of adventure might try this with an ESP32 microcontroller instead of a Pi Zero.

insights.claim: The author argues an ESP32 microcontroller is probably the technically smarter choice for driving the Adafruit LED display than a Raspberry Pi Zero, since ESP32 natively supports Wi-Fi and I2C without requiring a full Debian Linux stack.
insights.speaker: Lee Hutchinson
insights.so_what: A practical engineering trade-off worth noting for hobbyist/embedded hardware selection: Pi's OS-level convenience versus ESP32's leaner, purpose-built fit for this class of task.
insights.quote: In fact, the ESP32 is probably the smarter choice for controlling the Adafruit display, and it comes with Wi-Fi and I2C support without dragging Debian along for the ride.

insights.claim: The author self-hosts a LAN-only Gitea server for source control and uses Gitea Actions (a self-hosted CI/CD workflow) to build and deploy release artifacts to the Raspberry Pi via a dedicated, limited-privilege service account, explicitly choosing self-hosted infrastructure over cloud CI/CD.
insights.speaker: Lee Hutchinson
insights.so_what: Reflects a broader hobbyist/engineer trend of self-hosting dev-ops tooling (Gitea, LAN-only NTP/apt mirrors) for privacy and control rather than relying on cloud CI/CD providers.
insights.quote: Deployment works via a Gitea action, whereby I push a tag to my local Gitea repo and a runner creates a release artifact and shoves it onto the Pi via a separate local service account that can only do deployment-related things.
insights.locator: section 'A clock past the wit of man', later paragraph
